scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Limbo dates back to the mid-to-late 1800s in Tobago, where it was performed at funeral wakes.
It is conjectured to be related to the African 'legba' or 'legua' game.
Some scholars, like Dr. Alan Rice, link the movement to the restricted spaces of slave ships, where captive Africans used dance to communicate and bond.
on_screen: Map: Trinidad and Tobago · Caribbean
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a ritual reflecting the cycle of life and death, the emergence from under the pole symbolized the triumph of life.
In contemporary Trinidad and Tobago, it is a point of national pride and a staple of the Carnival season.
Globally, it has transitioned into a social 'icebreaker' used to animate social gatherings and tropical-themed events.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: The Man Who Can (https://archive.org/details/TheManWhoCan)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers approach a horizontal bar and must pass under it with their backs facing the floor.
The body must bend backwards without any part other than the feet touching the ground.
Turning the head or neck to the side is prohibited.
Watch for The Fire Pass, Human Bar.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Linear path moving forward under a fixed horizontal obstacle.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is traditionally performed to specific Afro-Caribbean drum patterns.
In the 1950s and 60s, it became associated with Calypso and Jamaican mento, often utilizing a clave rhythm.
Listen for the Drums, Steelpan, Guitar, Percussion.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 120 beats a minute.
A driving, syncopated percussion-heavy sound characterized by the bright timbre of steelpans and a steady, mid-tempo beat that facilitates rhythmic shuffling.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: While historically performed at wakes, modern Limbo is seen at festivals, Carnival, and tourist resorts.
Performers often wear vibrant Caribbean festival attire.
A key 'prop' introduced in the 1950s is the flaming limbo bar, where the horizontal pole is set on fire to increase the spectacle.
on_screen: Image gallery: 4 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Julia Edwards is the most significant figure, credited with professionalizing the dance and touring it globally.
Edric Connor is noted for reviving the game in 1944.
While originating in Tobago, the dance spread to Trinidad and became a national symbol.
Limbo is part of the Afro-Caribbean folk tradition, sharing roots with other African-derived games and rituals.
